name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQI_MAGNETISMANDMATTER_MCQ_Q51 - Magnetic moment of a current carrying toroid

questiontext.text: A toroid of \(n\) turns, mean radius \(R\) and cross-sectional radius \(a\) carries current \(I\). It is placed on a horizontal table taken as \(x\)-\(y\) plane. Its magnetic moment \(\mathbf{m}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A toroid is a hollow circular ring on which a large number of turns of a wire are closely wound. According to Ampere's circuital law, \(\oint \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = \mu_0 I_{\text{en}}\), the magnetic field produced by an ideal toroid is completely confined within the interior core of the toroid in the form of concentric circular field lines.

Step 2: Evaluation
For any circular Amperian loop drawn outside the toroid in the \(x\)-\(y\) plane, the net current enclosed is zero because each turn passes through the interior of the loop twice in opposite directions. Consequently, the magnetic field outside the toroid is zero everywhere.

Step 3: Application
A system possessing a non-zero net magnetic dipole moment \(\mathbf{m}\) produces a magnetic field at large distances \(r\) that falls off as \(\frac{1}{r^3}\). Since the magnetic field outside a toroid is zero, it cannot have a net magnetic dipole moment. Equivalently, summing the vector magnetic moments of all small current loops distributed symmetrically around the circular ring yields zero due to circular symmetry.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the magnetic moment \(\mathbf{m}\) of the toroid is zero, otherwise there would be a field falling as \(\frac{1}{r^3}\) at large distances outside the toroid.

answer.text: is non-zero and points in the \(z\)-direction by symmetry.
points along the axis of the toroid (\(m = m\dot{\phi}\)).
is zero, otherwise there would be a field falling as \(\frac{1}{r^3}\) at large distances outside the toroid.
is pointing radially outwards.

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQI_MAGNETISMANDMATTER_MCQ_Q52 - Declination variation in Earth dipole model

questiontext.text: The magnetic field of Earth can be modelled by that of a point dipole placed at the centre of the Earth. The dipole axis makes an angle of \(11.3^\circ\) with the axis of Earth. At Mumbai, declination is nearly zero. Then,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Magnetic declination at a place is the angle between the geographic meridian (the vertical plane containing the geographic north-south axis) and the magnetic meridian (the vertical plane containing the magnetic dipole axis).

Step 2: Evaluation
In the point-dipole model, the magnetic dipole axis is tilted at an angle of \(11.3^\circ\) with respect to the Earth's rotation axis. The plane containing both the geographic axis and the dipole axis intersects the Earth's surface along a great circle where the geographic and magnetic meridians coincide, giving zero declination (such as at Mumbai, not Greenwich).

Step 3: Application
At other longitudes on the Earth's surface, the magnetic north pole appears tilted either to the east or to the west of the geographic north pole, depending on which side of the zero-declination plane the point lies. The maximum angular deviation between the two meridians equals the tilt angle of \(11.3^\circ\) on either side (east or west), and by symmetry the average declination over the entire Earth is zero.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the declination varies between \(11.3^\circ\text{ W}\) to \(11.3^\circ\text{ E}\).

answer.text: the declination varies between \(11.3^\circ\text{ W}\) to \(11.3^\circ\text{ E}\).
the least declination is \(0^\circ\).
the plane defined by dipole axis and Earth axis passes through Greenwich.
declination averaged over Earth must be always negative.

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQI_MAGNETISMANDMATTER_MCQ_Q53 - Domain alignment in a permanent magnet

questiontext.text: In a permanent magnet at room temperature

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A permanent magnet is made of a ferromagnetic material that retains its ferromagnetic properties for a long period of time at room temperature.

Step 2: Evaluation
Individual atoms or molecules in a ferromagnetic material possess a non-zero permanent magnetic dipole moment. Due to strong quantum-mechanical exchange interactions, neighbouring atomic dipoles spontaneously align themselves in a common direction over macroscopic regions called domains.

Step 3: Application
In an unmagnetised ferromagnetic sample, the domains are randomly oriented so that the net magnetic moment is zero. When magnetised to form a permanent magnet, the domains align in the direction of the magnetising field and remain aligned even after the external field is removed, so that at room temperature the domains are all perfectly aligned.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, in a permanent magnet at room temperature, domains are all perfectly aligned.

answer.text: magnetic moment of each molecule is zero.
the individual molecules have non-zero magnetic moment which are all perfectly aligned.
domains are partially aligned.
domains are all perfectly aligned.

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQI_MAGNETISMANDMATTER_MCQ_Q54 - Idealized capacitor and solenoid versus Gauss law

questiontext.text: Consider the two idealized systems: (i) a parallel plate capacitor with large plates and small separation and (ii) a long solenoid of length \(L \gg R\), radius of cross-section. In (i) \(\mathbf{E}\) is ideally treated as a constant between plates and zero outside. In (ii) magnetic field is constant inside the solenoid and zero outside. These idealised assumptions, however, contradict fundamental laws as below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Gauss's law for electrostatics, \(\oint \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \frac{q_{\text{en}}}{\varepsilon_0}\), electric field lines can originate on positive charges and terminate on negative charges. In contrast, Gauss's law for magnetism, \(\oint \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0\), requires that magnetic field lines always form continuous closed loops without starting or ending anywhere.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the idealised parallel plate capacitor, \(\mathbf{E}\) is constant between the plates and zero outside; this does not contradict Gauss's law for electrostatics because field lines start on the positive plate and end on the negative plate, though it does contradict \(\oint \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = 0\) for a rectangular loop straddling the plate edge.

Step 3: Application
In the idealised long solenoid, \(\mathbf{B}\) is assumed to be constant inside and strictly zero outside. Consider a closed Gaussian surface enclosing one end of the solenoid: magnetic field lines enter (or leave) through the cross-section inside the solenoid, while the flux through the rest of the surface outside is zero. This gives a non-zero net magnetic flux \(\oint \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S} \neq 0\), which directly contradicts Gauss's law for magnetic fields (magnetic field lines must close back outside the solenoid).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the idealised assumption for the long solenoid contradicts Gauss's law for magnetic fields.

answer.text: case (i) contradicts Gauss's law for electrostatic fields.
case (ii) contradicts Gauss's law for magnetic fields.
case (i) agrees with \(\oint \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = 0\).
case (ii) contradicts \(\oint \mathbf{H} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = I_{en}\)

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQI_MAGNETISMANDMATTER_MCQ_Q55 - Magnetisation of a paramagnetic sample via Curie law

questiontext.text: A paramagnetic sample shows a net magnetisation of \(8\text{ Am}^{-1}\) when placed in an external magnetic field of \(0.6\text{ T}\) at a temperature of \(4\text{ K}\). When the same sample is placed in an external magnetic field of \(0.2\text{ T}\) at a temperature of \(16\text{ K}\), the magnetisation will be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial magnetisation, \(M_1 = 8\text{ Am}^{-1}\); initial external magnetic field, \(B_1 = 0.6\text{ T}\); initial absolute temperature, \(T_1 = 4\text{ K}\).
Final external magnetic field, \(B_2 = 0.2\text{ T}\); final absolute temperature, \(T_2 = 16\text{ K}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The sample is paramagnetic and operates in the linear regime away from saturation, so Curie's law applies. Temperature is measured on the Kelvin scale.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to Curie's law, the magnetisation \(M\) of a paramagnetic material is directly proportional to the applied magnetic field \(B\) and inversely proportional to the absolute temperature \(T\):
\[M = C \frac{B}{T}\]
where \(C\) is the Curie constant of the sample. Hence,
\[\frac{M_2}{M_1} = \frac{B_2}{B_1} \times \frac{T_1}{T_2}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substituting the given values:
\[\frac{M_2}{8\text{ Am}^{-1}} = \frac{0.2\text{ T}}{0.6\text{ T}} \times \frac{4\text{ K}}{16\text{ K}}\]
\[\frac{M_2}{8\text{ Am}^{-1}} = \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{12}\]
\[M_2 = \frac{8}{12}\text{ Am}^{-1} = \frac{2}{3}\text{ Am}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since the magnetic field decreases by a factor of \(3\) and the temperature increases by a factor of \(4\), the magnetisation must decrease by a factor of \(3 \times 4 = 12\), which is physically consistent. The final magnetisation is \(\frac{2}{3}\text{ Am}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQII_MAGNETISMANDMATTER_MCQ_Q56 - Continuity of B and H across a magnetic surface

questiontext.text: \(S\) is the surface of a lump of magnetic material.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Magnetic induction \(\mathbf{B}\) obeys Gauss's law for magnetism (\( abla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\)), which means magnetic field lines always form continuous closed loops. The magnetic intensity \(\mathbf{H}\) is related to \(\mathbf{B}\) and magnetisation \(\mathbf{M}\) by \(\mathbf{B} = \mu_0(\mathbf{H} + \mathbf{M})\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Because magnetic monopoles do not exist, lines of \(\mathbf{B}\) cannot originate or terminate on any surface \(S\). Thus, lines of \(\mathbf{B}\) are necessarily continuous across the surface \(S\) of the magnetic material.

Step 3: Application
Inside the magnetic material, \(\mathbf{M} eq \mathbf{0}\), whereas outside in free space, \(\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{0}\). Taking the divergence of \(\mathbf{H} = rac{\mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} - \mathbf{M}\) gives \( abla \cdot \mathbf{H} = - abla \cdot \mathbf{M}\), meaning that the normal component of \(\mathbf{H}\) jumps across the boundary \(S\) wherever there is a surface magnetisation pole density. Therefore, lines of \(\mathbf{H}\) cannot all be continuous across \(S\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Hence, lines of \(\mathbf{B}\) are necessarily continuous across \(S\), while lines of \(\mathbf{H}\) cannot all be continuous across \(S\).

answer.text: Lines of \(\mathbf{B}\) are necessarily continuous across \(S\).
Some lines of \(\mathbf{B}\) must be discontinuous across \(S\).
Lines of \(\mathbf{H}\) are necessarily continuous across \(S\).
Lines of \(\mathbf{H}\) cannot all be continuous across \(S\).

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQII_MAGNETISMANDMATTER_MCQ_Q57 - Primary origins of magnetism in matter

questiontext.text: The primary origin(s) of magnetism lies in

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Magnetism in matter arises from moving electric charges and intrinsic magnetic dipole moments of elementary particles, primarily electrons.

Step 2: Evaluation
In an atom, electrons revolve around the nucleus in orbits, forming microscopic closed current loops known as atomic currents. In addition, each electron possesses an intrinsic angular momentum (spin) and an associated intrinsic spin magnetic dipole moment.

Step 3: Application
The Pauli exclusion principle governs the filling of quantum states and influences exchange interactions between electrons, while the polar nature of molecules relates to electric dipole moments rather than magnetic moments. Neither of these is the primary origin of magnetism itself; the fundamental sources are the orbital atomic currents and the intrinsic spin of the electron.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the primary origins of magnetism lie in atomic currents and the intrinsic spin of the electron.

answer.text: atomic currents.
Pauli exclusion principle.
polar nature of molecules.
intrinsic spin of electron.

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQII_MAGNETISMANDMATTER_MCQ_Q58 - Solenoid core heated beyond Curie temperature

questiontext.text: A long solenoid has \(1000\) turns per metre and carries a current of \(1\text{ A}\). It has a soft iron core of \(\mu_r = 1000\). The core is heated beyond the Curie temperature, \(T_c\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a long solenoid with \(n\) turns per unit length carrying current \(I\), the magnetic intensity is \(H = nI\), which depends only on the free current and geometry. The magnetic field inside the core is \(B = \mu_0 \mu_r H = \mu_0(H + M)\), where the magnetisation is \(M = \chi H = (\mu_r - 1)H\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Before heating (below \(T_c\)), \(H = 1000 \times 1 = 1000\text{ A m}^{-1}\). With \(\mu_r = 1000\), \(\chi = \mu_r - 1 \approx 10^3\), so \(M_{\text{below}} \approx 10^3 \times 1000 = 10^6\text{ A m}^{-1}\) and \(B_{\text{below}} = \mu_0 \mu_r H \approx 1.26\text{ T}\).

Step 3: Application
When heated beyond the Curie temperature \(T_c\), soft iron transitions from ferromagnetic to paramagnetic, where its magnetic susceptibility drops to a typical paramagnetic value of \(\chi_{\text{above}} \sim 10^{-5}\). Since the solenoid current is unchanged, \(H\) remains nearly unchanged at \(1000\text{ A m}^{-1}\). However, \(B_{\text{above}} \approx \mu_0 H \approx 1.26 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T}\) decreases drastically, and the magnetisation \(M_{\text{above}} = \chi_{\text{above}} H \sim 10^{-5} \times 10^3 = 10^{-2}\text{ A m}^{-1}\) diminishes by a factor of \(\frac{M_{\text{below}}}{M_{\text{above}}} \sim \frac{10^6}{10^{-2}} = 10^8\) without reversing direction.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the \(\mathbf{H}\) field in the solenoid is (nearly) unchanged while the \(\mathbf{B}\) field decreases drastically, and the magnetisation in the core diminishes by a factor of about \(10^8\).

answer.text: The \(\mathbf{H}\) field in the solenoid is (nearly) unchanged but the \(\mathbf{B}\) field decreases drastically.
The \(\mathbf{H}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) fields in the solenoid are nearly unchanged.
The magnetisation in the core reverses direction.
The magnetisation in the core diminishes by a factor of about \(10^8\).

questiontext.text: Essential difference between electrostatic shielding by a conducting shell and magnetostatic shielding is due to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrostatic shielding relies on the fact that electric field lines can terminate on charges and conductors possess free charges that redistribute to cancel the electric field inside a hollow conducting cavity.

Step 2: Evaluation
In magnetostatics, magnetic monopoles do not exist, so lines of \(\mathbf{B}\) always form closed loops and cannot end on any material or conductor.

Step 3: Application
Because lines of \(\mathbf{B}\) cannot be terminated, perfect magnetostatic shielding is not possible in the way electrostatic shielding is. Instead, magnetostatic shielding is achieved by enclosing the region with shells made of high-permeability ferromagnetic materials (such as soft iron), which attract and divert the magnetic field lines through the shell walls away from the interior region.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Thus, the essential difference arises because electrostatic field lines can end on charges and conductors have free charges, lines of \(\mathbf{B}\) cannot end on any material so perfect shielding is not possible, and shells of high permeability materials can be used to divert lines of \(\mathbf{B}\) from the interior region.

answer.text: electrostatic field lines can end on charges and conductors have free charges.
lines of \(\mathbf{B}\) can also end but conductors cannot end them.
lines of \(\mathbf{B}\) cannot end on any material and perfect shielding is not possible.
shells of high permeability materials can be used to divert lines of \(\mathbf{B}\) from the interior region.

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQII_MAGNETISMANDMATTER_MCQ_Q510 - Angle of dip on the geographical equator

questiontext.text: Let the magnetic field on earth be modelled by that of a point magnetic dipole at the centre of earth. The angle of dip at a point on the geographical equator

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The angle of dip (inclination) \(\delta\) is the angle that the Earth's total magnetic field vector makes with the horizontal surface of the Earth. For a point magnetic dipole, the angle of dip is zero everywhere on the magnetic equator (where the vertical component is zero).

Step 2: Evaluation
The Earth's magnetic dipole axis is tilted at an angle of approximately \(11.3^\circ\) with respect to the Earth's rotation axis. Consequently, the magnetic equator and the geographical equator are two distinct great circles that intersect at two diametrically opposite points.

Step 3: Application
At the two points of intersection, a point on the geographical equator also lies on the magnetic equator, so the angle of dip is zero at those specific points. Along the rest of the geographical equator, half of the circle lies in the northern magnetic hemisphere (where the dip angle is positive) and the other half lies in the southern magnetic hemisphere (where the dip angle is negative). Because the tilt is finite (\(11.3^\circ\)), the magnitude of the dip angle on the geographical equator cannot exceed a maximum value determined by \(\tan\delta = 2\tan(11.3^\circ)\), so it is bounded.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, at a point on the geographical equator, the angle of dip can be zero at specific points, can be positive or negative, and is bounded.

answer.text: is always zero.
can be zero at specific points.
can be positive or negative.
is bounded.
